units.text: From the encounter with Yathrib to the covenant at al-ʿAqaba
How did news of Islam reach Yathrib, and what changed between the first pledge and the covenant of protection?

The story begins with an encounter at al-ʿAqaba with men of Khazraj who carried news of the call to Yathrib. Twelve came to pledge allegiance in the following pilgrimage season, and then the Prophet ﷺ sent Muṣʿab to teach the people there. At a later meeting, the discussion turned to protecting him if he came to them: what had changed between the two covenants, and how did the people of Yathrib receive the teaching and the appointment?
An encounter whose news reached Yathrib

At al-ʿAqaba, the Prophet ﷺ met some men of Khazraj. They sat with him and heard his call and the Quran. In the account Ibn Isḥāq transmits from the elders cited by ʿĀṣim, they recognized what the Jews had been saying about a prophet soon to appear. They accepted Islam and hoped that through him God would unite their people, whom enmity had divided.

The men returned to Yathrib, calling their people to Islam. Ibn Isḥāq says that they were six men of Khazraj and that mention of the Prophet ﷺ spread through the households of the Anṣār. In the following pilgrimage season came the delegation for the First Pledge of al-ʿAqaba.
Twelve men and a pledge before warfare

In the following pilgrimage season, twelve men met the Prophet ﷺ at al-ʿAqaba and pledged allegiance in what Ibn Isḥāq calls the Pledge of the Women, before warfare was prescribed, according to this account. ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit mentions renouncing idolatry, theft, adultery, the killing of children, and false accusation, and not disobeying the Prophet ﷺ in what is right. This was not yet the pledge to defend and protect him that would come at the later meeting.
Muṣʿab: teaching and the response

After those who had pledged departed, the Prophet ﷺ sent Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr with them to recite the Quran to them, teach them Islam, and instruct them in the religion. He stayed with Asʿad ibn Zurāra and led the people in prayer; a continuation transmitted by ʿĀṣim says that some of Aws and Khazraj disliked having members of the other group lead them in prayer.

Asʿad took Muṣʿab toward the quarters of Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal and Banū Ẓafar, and they entered an orchard belonging to Banū Ẓafar, as Ibn Isḥāq relates from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Mughīra and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr. Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr came to prevent them from preaching among his people. Muṣʿab invited him to sit and listen, promising that they would stop doing what displeased him if he was not satisfied. Usayd sat, heard the Quran and embraced Islam; he then returned to Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, who came to the two men in turn.

Saʿd arrived angry. When Muṣʿab invited him to listen, he sat down and accepted Islam after hearing the Quran. He returned to Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal and called them to faith; the account says that they embraced Islam. Muṣʿab then remained with Asʿad, calling the people, and Islam spread among the households of the Anṣār, except for certain households whose people, the account says, Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat kept from embracing Islam.
The meeting for protection: who would bear the consequences?

Muṣʿab returned to Mecca, and Muslims among the Anṣār set out with their people's pilgrims for an agreed meeting at al-ʿAqaba. Kaʿb ibn Mālik, who attended it, relates that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥarām embraced Islam after they told him of the appointment. Then they slipped away from their camps; according to his account, those assembled were seventy-three men accompanied by two women.

Al-ʿAbbās, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, attended; Kaʿb describes him as still following his people's religion at the time. He asked the group to weigh their ability to fulfill their undertaking and protect the Prophet ﷺ after he came to them. The Prophet ﷺ then recited the Quran and proposed a pledge that they would protect him as they protected their women and children. Al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr declared their acceptance of this protection.

Abū al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihān asked: if they severed their ties with the Jews and then God granted the Prophet ﷺ victory, would he return to his own people and abandon them? His answer in Kaʿb's account was: “I am of you and you are of me. I fight those whom you fight and make peace with those with whom you make peace.” The Prophet ﷺ then requested twelve leaders responsible for their people; nine were chosen from Khazraj and three from Aws.
The leaders' covenant and the morning after al-ʿAqaba

In Ibn Isḥāq's transmission from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr, the Prophet ﷺ addresses the leaders as guarantors for their people. In an account transmitted by ʿĀṣim, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿUbāda warns those pledging not to hand over the Prophet ﷺ when they suffer loss of property or the killing of their nobles. The people replied that they accepted the covenant on those terms. They asked what they would receive if they fulfilled it, and the Prophet ﷺ answered: Paradise.

After the pledge, the Prophet ﷺ ordered the people back to their camps. When al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿUbāda offered to fight the people of Minā the next day, he answered that they had not been commanded to do so. The following morning, leading men of Quraysh questioned the delegation about reports of the pledge. The polytheists among the delegation denied knowing of it, and Kaʿb says they had not known. Ibn Isḥāq then gives another account of Quraysh questioning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, followed by a continuation saying they verified the report and set off in pursuit of the delegation. They caught up with Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda and al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr and seized Saʿd after al-Mundhir escaped.
From the pledge of the women to the covenant of protection

In Ibn Isḥāq's wording, the “Pledge of the Women” at the first meeting belongs to a time before warfare was prescribed. By contrast, the undertaking to protect the Prophet ﷺ as they protected their women and children comes in Kaʿb's account of the later meeting.

In the version from ʿUbāda that Ibn Isḥāq relates through Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb, the fate of anyone who commits one of the prohibited acts rests with God: He may punish or forgive. In the version he gives through al-Zuhrī from ʿUbāda, having the prescribed penalty imposed in this world is an expiation, while the matter of a person whose act remains concealed rests with God. The provisions agree in ʿUbāda’s two versions, but the conclusions about consequences differ; neither is the text of the covenant of protection at the later meeting.

On the road to the pilgrimage, al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr differed from his companions and prayed toward the Kaaba while they prayed toward Syria. Kaʿb says that he asked the Prophet ﷺ, then returned to his previous prayer direction and prayed with them toward Syria. Kaʿb also reports that al-Barāʾ's family claim he continued praying toward the Kaaba until he died, and disputes their claim.
Al-ʿAbbās’s intent and the first to pledge

ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda explains al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿUbāda’s warning as an attempt to strengthen the covenant for the Prophet ﷺ; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr says he wanted to delay the group in the hope that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy would attend. The account concludes that God knows best which it was. Al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿUbāda is not al-ʿAbbās, the Prophet’s ﷺ uncle, who spoke about the guarantee of protection in Kaʿb’s account.

Ibn Isḥāq lists the names of the six as they were related to him. Amid the list are three comments by Ibn Hishām: an identification concerning ʿAfrāʾ, a possible name for ʿĀmir ibn al-Azraq, and a correction to Sawād's genealogy. Ibn Hishām also offers an explanation of the word “al-hadm” in the Prophet's ﷺ answer at the other meeting. This later explanation is not part of the Prophet's words.
Accounts differ over who first struck the Prophet’s ﷺ hand in pledging: Banū al-Najjār name Asʿad, Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal name Abū al-Haytham, and Kaʿb names al-Barāʾ.

Ibn Isḥāq said: When God, mighty and exalted, willed to make His religion manifest, strengthen His Prophet ﷺ, and fulfill His promise to him, the Messenger of God ﷺ went out in the pilgrimage season when he met the group of Anṣār. As in every pilgrimage season, he presented himself to the Arab tribes. While he was at al-ʿAqaba, he met a group of Khazraj for whom God intended good.

(He said) [2]: When morning came, the leading men of Quraysh came to us in our lodgings. They said, “People of Khazraj, we have heard that you have come to this companion of ours to take him out from among us and pledge to fight us.
